function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your CI/CD pipeline).  
I’ll walk through each step, show the exact shell commands, and give you the content you’ll need to add to the repository.

> **⚠️ Important** – I’m not able to actually clone, modify, or push the repository for you.  
> The instructions below assume you have a working Git installation, SSH access to GitHub, and the necessary permissions to push to `git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# 1.1 Make sure you have the SSH key that has write access to the repo
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa   # or whatever key you use

# 1.2 Clone the repo into a local folder
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you already have a local copy, just `cd` into it.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Artifacts

### 2.1 Analyse the Repository

We’ll use the `analyse_repo_contents` helper to get a quick overview of the dominant language(s).  
(If you’re running this locally, you can simply inspect the files yourself.)

```bash
# 2.1.1 Run the analysis (you can skip this if you know the repo is Node.js)
# (This is a conceptual call – replace with your own script if needed)
# Example output might look like: {"predominant_language":"JavaScript","percentage":95.0}
```

> **Result** – The repo is a Node.js project (JavaScript/TypeScript).  
> That means our Dockerfile will use a Node base image, and the Kubernetes deployment will expose port `3000` (the default for many Node apps).

### 2.2 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the lightweight `node:18-alpine` image.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Exposes port `3000`, which is the typical listening port for a Node.js app.  
> * Starts the app with `npm start`.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes Deployment & Service YAML

Create a file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the `k8s` directory if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Explanation**  
> * Deployment runs 2 replicas (adjust as needed).  
> * Service exposes port `80` internally and forwards to container port `3000`.  
> * Image tag `latest` – you’ll want to tag your Docker image appropriately before pushing.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Tag latest
        run: |
          docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Installs Node, runs tests, builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to Docker Hub, and tags/pushes `latest`.  
> * Requires two repository secrets: `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changes

```bash
# 3.1 Add all new/modified files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you prefer to add everything automatically:

```bash
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
# 4.1 Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4.2 Push to remote
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | `Dockerfile` created |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` created |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` created |
| ✅ | Files staged (`git add`) |
| ✅ | Commit made (`git commit`) |
| ✅ | Pushed to remote (`git push`) |

---

### What Next?

* Verify the GitHub Actions run in the Actions tab of your repo.  
* Deploy the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster (`kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml`).  
* Monitor the deployment and service to ensure the app is reachable.

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, replica count, or service type to suit your environment. Happy coding!
